prompt:
I need the front end for Minutebank. An in-house archive of board and committee minutes, resolutions and action items, built for the Corporate Secretary's office of a large regional passenger railway operator.

Who's using it: Theo Lindqvist, an assistant corporate secretary who joined the office eighteen months ago. He knows the committee structure well, but not the history of decisions made before his time, and he writes fast, precise internal memos for the General Counsel.

What they're doing right now: The board's Capital Projects Committee meets in nine days to decide whether to renew the depot electrification program, and the committee chair has asked for a short history of every past decision on it: when it was first approved, budget changes, conditions attached, and actions that were assigned but never closed. Theo searched 'electrification' and got 212 documents going back to 2015, most of which only mention it in passing. He needs to cut that down to the dozen or so minutes and resolutions where something was actually decided, read each one closely, and pull exact resolution numbers and wording.

What's in the system at this point: About 4,300 documents from 2015–2026: minutes, resolutions, consent agendas and action-item records from the full Board and six committees (Capital Projects, Audit & Risk, Safety, Finance, Governance, Customer & Service). Each has a meeting date, committee, document type, status (draft, approved, superseded), confidentiality level (public, board-only, privileged), page count, and attachments. Resolutions have numbers like CPC-2019-14 and outcomes (adopted, amended, deferred, withdrawn) plus vote counts. Action items have an owner, due date and status (open, closed, overdue); 7 electrification-related items are still open, the oldest from March 2021. The 212 hits include 38 Capital Projects minutes, 11 resolutions mentioning 'Northgate Depot' or 'Eastyard Depot', budget figures ranging from $48M (2017 approval) to $112M (2023 amendment), and 4 superseded drafts that duplicate approved versions.

Build it as a working web app, opened in the state that person would see at that moment. No backend: use realistic mock data (no lorem ipsum, no placeholder names), and make the interactive parts actually work client-side.

Use whatever framework and tooling you like. When you're done there must be a static production build in ./out with ./out/index.html as the entry point. It will be served from the root of a plain static file server (no rewrites, no server code) and viewed in a desktop browser at 1440×900.
